payload.task_text:
I am working on my PhD thesis and I need help putting together the literature review section for Chapter 2, which focuses on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In my workspace there is a compressed archive called research_notes.tar.gz that contains some preliminary notes I have been keeping in markdown files about background concepts, key research questions, and related retrieval methods. I would appreciate it if you could first extract that archive so we can see what is in there, and then read through the notes to understand the context of my research.

My research focus and the key concepts I am tracking are stored in a knowledge graph file located at memory/memory.json in the workspace. Please read that to understand the scope and direction of my literature review.

After familiarizing yourself with my notes and research focus, I need you to search academic databases for recent and foundational papers on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. I am looking for approximately five key papers that cover the topic from different angles, including the original RAG formulation, survey papers, self-reflective retrieval approaches, recursive retrieval methods, and practical system-building perspectives. For each paper you find, please download it and read through its content to understand the main contributions. I would also like you to look at the source manuscripts of these papers to examine the methodology sections in more detail, since the methodology comparison is an important part of my literature review.

Once you have gathered all of this information, please store the key findings in my knowledge graph so that I can reference them later. Then create a Word document called Literature_Review.docx in my workspace. The document should begin with an introduction section that provides an overview of Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a research area and explains why it matters for knowledge-intensive natural language processing tasks. Following the introduction, include a dedicated section for each of the five papers you found. Each paper section should clearly state the paper title, the authors, the publication year, a description of the main contribution, and a discussion of the methodology used. After covering all five papers, end the document with a conclusion section that synthesizes the key themes, identifies common patterns across the papers, and suggests directions for future research. Please make sure the writing flows naturally and reads like a proper academic literature review rather than a collection of disconnected summaries.

A few things to keep in mind while you work.

First, the databases may return papers that are not actually about Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including papers from other fields. Judge each result by its title and abstract. The review should cover only the papers that are genuinely about RAG; please do not include or discuss unrelated papers in Literature_Review.docx.

Second, the deliverable is a single file, Literature_Review.docx, and it must end up complete and well-formed. It must be created exactly once, by exactly one designated agent, and only after all of the paper content has been gathered. Any agent that is responsible for only a portion of this task (for example, researching a subset of the papers) must NOT create, write, overwrite, or append to Literature_Review.docx; that agent should instead return its findings in its report or write them to its own separately named intermediate file that no other agent writes to. Do not have several agents append to or rewrite the same document file, as that will corrupt or overwrite it. A safe way to work in parallel is to have each agent take responsibility for a distinct subset of the papers and return its findings, and then have one agent assemble the final document exactly once, after all of the findings are in.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one research wave. The main agent must extract `research_notes.tar.gz` once without overwriting files, read the extracted Markdown and `memory/memory.json`, and freeze these five non-overlapping topics: original RAG formulation; RAG survey; self-reflective/adaptive retrieval; recursive/hierarchical retrieval; and practical system building.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Explore 0 owns only the original RAG formulation topic.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Explore 1 owns only the strongest RAG survey topic.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Explore 2 owns only self-reflective or adaptive retrieval.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Explore 3 owns only recursive or hierarchical retrieval.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Explore 4 owns only practical RAG system building.

Each explore sub-agent searches only its assigned topic, rejects off-topic titles/abstracts, selects exactly one distinct paper, downloads and reads that paper, inspects the available LaTeX methodology sections, and writes one uniquely named compact evidence JSON containing topic, stable ID, exact title, authors, year, contribution, methodology, evidence section names, and limitations. Return only the JSON path, stable ID, and compact search/read controls. No sub-agent may modify the knowledge graph or create `Literature_Review.docx`.

After Wave 1, the main agent verifies five distinct IDs and five topic slots, then directly owns both remaining outputs. Update the existing knowledge graph by adding only the five source-supported paper entities and relationships while preserving unrelated nodes. Create `Literature_Review.docx` exactly once with one bulk structured write: title; Introduction; five sections in the frozen topic order, each stating the exact title, authors, year, main contribution, and methodology; and a synthetic Conclusion with common themes and future research. Use only the five retained papers, exclude all rejected results, read the graph and document back once, and finish without another sub-agent or verification wave.

nodes.text:
Research exactly five genuine Retrieval-Augmented Generation papers for a PhD literature review, covering these distinct angles: (1) original RAG formulation, (2) major RAG survey, (3) self-reflective retrieval (Self-RAG), (4) recursive/hierarchical retrieval (RAPTOR or equivalent), and (5) practical system-building/engineering perspective. Context from thesis notes: focus on retrieval relevance and efficiency, retrieval granularity, factual accuracy, attribution/faithfulness, and methodology comparison; project also tracks venue and citation counts where reliably obtainable. Search academic databases, judge relevance by title/abstract, select canonical papers, and provide complete metadata (exact title, authors, year, venue/status, arXiv ID/DOI as available). For each selected paper, download/store it using the arxiv_local download tool and read the full paper. Also inspect its source manuscript, especially methodology, using arxiv-latex section tools. Return an independently verifiable report with: selection rationale, abstract-based relevance check, detailed main contributions, methodology (architecture, retrieval corpus/index, retrieval/generation process, training/objective, datasets/tasks, evaluation), key results, limitations, and cross-paper methodological comparison. Explicitly report successful download status and exact arXiv IDs. Do not create or modify Literature_Review.docx or any workspace file; return findings only. If citation counts cannot be verified via available sources, clearly say so rather than inventing them.
Research five RAG papers

Create exactly one new Word document at `/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/Literature_Review.docx`. You are the sole designated creator. Do not create the file in stages under that name and do not overwrite it if it already exists; first verify it does not exist, compose content in memory or a separately named temporary artifact if needed, then create the final DOCX exactly once. Produce a polished academic literature review for Chapter 2 on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, with title, Introduction, one dedicated section for each of the five papers below, a cross-paper synthesis woven naturally into the discussion, and Conclusion/Future Research. Each paper section must explicitly state exact title, authors, year, main contribution, and detailed methodology. Include venue/status and canonical arXiv identifier where supplied. Do not include RAGAS; the fifth paper is the practical systems paper below. Ensure cohesive prose, methodological comparison, factual accuracy vs faithfulness distinction, retrieval relevance/efficiency/granularity, evaluation, and attribution. Include a final References section. Avoid unsupported citation counts.

Use these verified findings:
1) Lewis et al., `Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks`, Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela; 2020, NeurIPS 2020, arXiv 2005.11401. Original RAG: DPR bi-encoder retrieves top-k from Dec. 2018 English Wikipedia (~21m ~100-word passages, dense FAISS/MIPS index); BART generator; latent-document marginal likelihood; RAG-Sequence uses document mixture at sequence level, RAG-Token at token level; query encoder and generator fine-tuned. Tasks Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC, MS MARCO, Jeopardy question generation, FEVER. Reported 44.5 EM on NQ. Limits: static corpus/chunking, latency, no entailment/attribution guarantee.
2) Gao et al., `Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey`, Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Haofen Wang; 2023 preprint, arXiv 2312.10997. Survey taxonomy: Naive, Advanced, Modular RAG; lifecycle indexing/retrieval/augmentation/generation; query rewriting, sparse/dense/hybrid retrieval, reranking, compression, iterative/recursive/adaptive retrieval; discusses RGB, RECALL, CRUD and relevance, faithfulness, correctness, latency/cost. Survey methodology, not a trained system; limitation is fast-moving/heterogeneous evidence.
3) Asai et al., `Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection`, Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi; 2024, ICLR 2024, canonical arXiv 2310.11511. Adaptive retrieval; special Retrieve, ISREL, ISSUP, ISUSE tokens. Critic annotates training data; generator fine-tuned by next-token prediction on augmented sequences; at inference selectively retrieves passage evidence and scores relevance/support/utility without critic. Tasks include PopQA, TriviaQA, reasoning, verification, long-form generation. Local record reports 54.9 PopQA vs 51.2 standard RAG and 44.0 ChatGPT in setup. Limits critic noise, fallible reflection, complexity, retriever/corpus dependence.
4) Sarthi et al., `RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval`, Parth Sarthi, Salman Abdullah, Aditi Tuli, Shubh Khanna, Anna Goldie, Christopher D. Manning; 2024, ICLR 2024, canonical arXiv 2401.18059. Split documents into leaves, embed, dimensionality reduction, Gaussian-mixture soft clustering, LLM summaries become parents recursively; retrieve via top-down traversal or collapsed-tree search over all levels; pretrained components, no central end-to-end joint training. NarrativeQA, QASPER, QuALITY. Local record reports 30.87 METEOR on NarrativeQA with GPT-4 vs 23.52 chunk retrieval. Limits index cost, summary distortions/error propagation, update complexity, attribution challenge.
5) Chen et al., `From RAG to Rich: Building Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems`, Wenqi Chen, Jialin Wu, Dawei Zhu, Xiaoguang Li, Shuaiyi Nie; 2024 preprint, local arXiv record 2404.10981. Practical engineering lifecycle in five pillars: ingestion (parsing/chunking/metadata), indexing (embeddings/vector DB/hybrid BM25), retrieval (query understanding/multi-stage/reranking), generation (prompts/context/citations), evaluation (automated/human/regression). Ablations in legal, medical, technical documentation; inspected record says chunking up to 23% improvement, embedding choice 15%, reranking 12%, hybrid beats either alone. Discuss caveat that implementation/domain choices affect transferability.

Thesis context from notes: RAG grounds generators in external, updateable, domain knowledge; research questions concern relevant and efficient context, retrieval granularity (sentence/paragraph/document/summary), factual accuracy, attribution, retrieval relevance, faithfulness, latency and complexity. Dense retrieval (DPR), late interaction (ColBERT), sparse BM25, hybrid retrieval, query decomposition, iterative retrieval are relevant context.

Styling acceptance: professional academic Word document, readable hierarchy, consistent body font, page numbers if practical, no malformed placeholders, and complete references. Verify the final DOCX can be opened/read and report its path and basic structure. Do not modify memory.json or any paper resources.
